headlines.article_text: Musk: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production in Texas next year Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Elon Musk said Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production at Gigafactory Texas around mid-2027. Musk said the change will make room for increased production of Tesla’s Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales and has faced several recalls. A Tesla Cybertruck at the company's store in Colma, California, US, on Monday, April 21, 2025. David Paul Morris | Bloomberg | Getty Images Tesla CEO Elon Musk on Friday said the electric vehicle maker will "be winding down" production of the Cybertruck at its Texas gigafactory around the middle of next year. Musk , who hailed the Cybertruck as the future of the pickup truck segment , said in a post on X early Friday morning that the end of production at the massive facility would make room for production of its Cybercab robotaxi. The Cybertruck is exclusively produced at the company's plant in Texas alongside the Tesla Model Y and two-seat Cybercab, which Musk has touted as a crucial product for the automaker moving forward. Musk did not say whether the company would produce the Cybertruck at a different facility, but he later responded to a user on X who called the update an "end of an era" and said the Cybertruck was the "best vehicle Tesla has ever made." "True, but the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time," Musk said. Tesla began Cybertruck deliveries in late 2023 . The company did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNBC. watch now VIDEO 12:23 12:23 Why Cybertruck sales have struggled Autos The Cybertruck and its polarizing design gained a niche following, but it did not achieve mass-market sales, despite Musk's pre-launch prediction that annual sales would eventually total 250,000. "Trucks have been the same for a very long time," Musk said when the truck was unveiled in 2019. "Like 100 years. Trucks have been basically the same. We want to try something different." While Tesla does not break out its sales by model or region, Cox Automotive estimated sales of the Cybertruck last year at 20,237 units in the U.S., down 48% from 38,965 in 2024. One big buyer of the Cybertruck last year was Elon Musk's aerospace and tech conglomerate, SpaceX , which spent $131 million buying up the angular steel trucks at Tesla's suggested retail price, according to a SpaceX financial filing . The distinct look of the vehicle made some owners a target of rude gestures and more serious road rage, one owner told CNBC last May , after Musk became the biggest funder of Donald Trump's presidential campaign and led the Department of Government Efficiency, an effort to slash the federal workforce and regulations. Wired wrote in an October 2025 feature story, "There is likely no object that feels more emblematic of US president Donald Trump's return to the White House than the Tesla Cybertruck ." The magazine interviewed owners who described being spit on and sworn at due to their choice of vehicle. The Cybertruck's specifications also fell short of those Tesla advertised early on, and in some cases fell short of those offered by leading fuel-burning pickups. There have also been many quality and production problems associated with the vehicles. The 2024 Tesla Cybertruck was the subject of 11 voluntary recalls, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration website. Issues ranged from a "trapped" acceleration pedal risk that could cause unintended acceleration, to software defects and an inverter fault that could result in sudden loss of drive power. Michael Nagle | Bloomberg | Getty Images The Nasdaq Composite plunged into correction territory on Thursday. History shows more selling can follow in the near term, but a recovery eventually takes hold three months later. The tech-heavy index slid more than 5% on Thursday, closing more than 11% below its record reached last month. On Wall Street, any decline greater than 10% is a correction. A 20% pullback qualifies as a bear market. Across 10 previous correction episodes over the last decade, selloffs in 2025, 2022, 2020 and 2018 were followed by further rough selling over the next one month. But the Nasdaq was back to rally mode again after six months for all those occasions except one: 2022. Overall, the Nasdaq gained an average of 9.41% from the correction bottom over the following three months and 17.03% over six months. The January 2022 correction was the one that offered a harsher outcome. The Nasdaq lost another 18.3% over the next six months and was down 24.3% a year later. Nasdaq Composite Deena Zaidi and Nick Wells The catalyst for this correction was Democrats sweeping the House and Senate in Tuesday's midterm elections. The party also made significant gains in Texas, where Gina Hinojosa won the race for governor after campaigning on an immediate moratorium for data center development. Investors are now weighing whether tighter state-level restrictions could slow data center construction, putting pressure on companies tied to the artificial intelligence trade. Frank Cappelleri, founder of CappThesis, pointed to past midterm election cycles for guidance and found that points to more volatility in the near term as well. The chart analyst said the Nasdaq was higher 12 months after the election in all but one of 13 midterm cycles since 1974. "The caveat is that the path can be a volatile one," he said. Cappelleri pointed to 2018, when the Nasdaq rallied the day after Democrats won the House. A sharp December sell-off followed, but the index was ultimately about 15% higher a year after the election, he said. headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves premarket: Moderna, Airbnb, Cloudflare, Affirm & more Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Check out some of the companies making the biggest moves premarket: Moderna — The vaccine maker rallied nearly 10%. The company smashed third-quarter earnings and estimates and raised its outlook for full-year sales growth. Moderna now expects 2026 revenue growth of 15% to 25%, up from previous guidance of no more than 10%. Lam Research — The semiconductor equipment maker surged nearly 11% after the board authorized a $25 billion stock buyback. Five9 — The cloud-based Contact Center as a Service provider fell more than 17% premarket. Five9 lowered full-year adjusted EPS guidance and announced a $325 million cash acquisition of Level AI. Affirm Holdings — The buy now pay later lender dropped 4%. Affirm posted quarterly results and released forward guidance above expectations and raised its full-year gross merchandise volume outlook, but credit concerns remained an overhang. Axon Enterprise — The Taser maker dropped nearly 9% after third-quarter EPS and revenue missed Wall Street estimates, fourth-quarter guidance was weak and it pledged an additional $1.2 billion investment in drone maker Skydio, raising its stake to about 37%. AI and semiconductor stocks — Micron Technology, Sandisk , Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices Nebius and CoreWeave climbed pre-market trading Friday, recovering ground after Thursday's sharp selloff amid concerns over potential constraints on AI data-center expansion. Cloudflare — Shares climbed 19% pre-market after guidance for the current quarter topped Street expectations. Cloudflare forecast adjusted earnings of 43 cents a share versus a FactSet consensus for 38 cents, on revenue of $845-$846 million, higher than analysts' consensus of $796 million. Iren – The neocloud provider jumped nearly 19% after fiscal first-quarter revenue of $228 million grew from $137 million the prior quarter. More than $4 billion in annual recurring revenue projected to arrive in 2026 has been delayed until at least January 2027. Iren has been battered in the latest rout of AI-focused stocks, dropping 31% in the past week. Airbnb — The online lodging marketplace jumped 13% after third-quarter earnings of $3.16 per share topped analysts' consensus estimate of $2.85. Revenue of $4.87 billion beat the Street's $4.75 billion estimate, LSEG data showed. Atlassian — Shares dropped more than 18% after the supplier of team collaboration and productivity software showed year-over-year data center revenue growth expected to decline approximately 14% in the fiscal second quarter ending in December, and 16% in the fiscal year ending next June. JFrog — The software company soared 23% premarket after raising full-year guidance. JFrog sees adjusted earnings ranging from $1.14 to $1.16 per share on revenue of $680 million to $682 million. The outlook trounced FactSet consensus estimates of 98 cents a share and $651.9 million. DraftKings — The online sports betting platform tumbled more than 20% premarket. DraftKings posted a wider-than-expected third-quarter loss of 94 cents per share, worse than the 39 cent loss analysts polled by LSEG anticipated. Revenue of $1.33 billion fell short of the $1.40 billion estimate. Sportsbook revenue totaled $784 million, missing the $811.8 million StreetAccount consensus estimate. Lyft — The ridesharing company fell more than 5%. Third-quarter revenue of $1.82 billion trailed the FactSet consensus among analysts for $1.92 billion, while fourth-quarter guidance for bookings came in at $5.74 billion to $5.94 billion versus the FactSet consensus of $5.81 billion. — CNBC's Darla Mercado and Scott Schnipper contributed reporting
